How thinking changes

Week 3 · Chapter 2 · Cognitive and Language Development

Study · Week 3

Read Chapter 2 of the textbook (Eggen & Kauchak, 2025) first, then this. Three theorists, and they are not three versions of the same idea — they disagree about where thinking comes from.

About 20 minutes: reading, one place you stop and write, and 8 quick checks.

Pair this with the Walkthrough — 14 minutes of me working the case through one lens, and arguing myself out of my first answer.

The claim you already believe

That children are small adults who know less, and development is the process of filling up. If that were true, teaching would be a delivery problem.

The case against it is in your own life. Think of something you understand now that you could not have understood at fourteen — not a fact you lacked, but a kind of thinking that was unavailable to you. Most people find one in seconds.

You did not acquire that by being told it.

Piaget: the comfort zone and its disruption

Chapter 2 gives you the machinery. It is worth learning in this form, because you will use it every week for the rest of the semester:

Developmentally ready — pre-assess where students actually are Not where the curriculum says they should be. This is a measurement, not an assumption.

Schema — an existing conceptual framework What is already in there, doing the interpreting.

Equilibrium — the comfort zone New information fits. Nothing has to change.

Disequilibrium — disruption of the comfort zone It does not fit. This is uncomfortable, and it is the engine of the whole system.

Assimilation — expansion of the comfort zone The new case is folded into the schema you already had. Cheap.

Accommodation — transformation of the comfort zone The schema itself is rebuilt. Expensive, and it is what learning actually is.

Rejection — denial, bias, dissonance The evidence is discarded so the schema can survive. Also cheap. Also extremely common.

True or false?

Assimilation is when a learner rebuilds a schema to fit new information.

Not quite Rebuilding is accommodation. Assimilation folds the new case into the schema you already had, and nothing gets rebuilt.

Right Assimilation stretches the schema. Accommodation rebuilds it.

Three things can happen when new information does not fit: you stretch the schema (assimilate), you rebuild it (accommodate), or you throw the information away (reject). Only one of those is learning, and it is the only one that costs anything.

Rejection is not in most textbook summaries, and it should be. It explains why demonstrating that someone is wrong so often produces a more confident version of the same belief. If accommodation is expensive enough, rejection is the rational move — and your students make it constantly, about your subject.

Check yourself

A student who says “I’m just not a math person” solves a hard problem correctly, then says it was luck. In Piaget’s terms, this is:

Something was discarded Assimilation folds the case in. Here the evidence is explained away.

The schema survived Accommodation would mean rebuilding the belief. “Luck” keeps it intact.

Yes The evidence is thrown out so the schema can survive. Cheap, comfortable and very common.

There was a mismatch The correct answer did not fit the belief. That is disequilibrium, resolved by rejection.

Commit first

You have designed a lesson that makes students genuinely uncomfortable — their existing belief about your topic clearly does not work on the case you have given them. Half the class is frustrated. One student says “can you just tell us the answer?”

Has your lesson failed? Two or three sentences.

It is working. Whether it succeeds depends entirely on what you do in the next ten minutes.

Disequilibrium is the condition under which accommodation becomes possible. A lesson where nobody is uncomfortable is a lesson where every student assimilated — the new material was absorbed into what they already thought, and nothing was rebuilt.

But discomfort alone does not produce accommodation. It produces a choice between three outcomes, and the two cheap ones are always available. Sustained frustration with no path forward reliably produces rejection — this subject is stupid, I’m just not a maths person — which is a stable, comfortable resolution that costs the student nothing.

So the answer to “can you just tell us?” is neither yes nor no. It is a scaffold: enough support that rebuilding is now the cheapest available option.

Which is exactly where Vygotsky comes in.

Vygotsky: thinking is social first

Piaget’s child is a lone scientist, running experiments on the world and revising private theories. Vygotsky’s disagreement is fundamental: higher mental functions begin between people and only later move inside.

Zone of proximal development — what a learner can do with support but not yet alone Not what they can already do. Not what is hopelessly beyond them. The band in between, where teaching does anything at all.

True or false?

The zone of proximal development is the set of tasks a learner can already do alone.

Not quite What a learner can do alone is the inner circle. The ZPD is the ring around it: what they can do with support but not yet alone.

Right The ZPD is the band between alone and not yet: what they can do with support.

Scaffolding — support calibrated to the learner, and withdrawn as competence grows Three properties: progressive, differential, faded. A scaffold that never comes down is not a scaffold — it is a dependency.

The zone moves. It is not a property of the student, it is a property of the student-plus-task-plus-support at a moment in time. Yesterday’s zone is today’s independent work, and a scaffold left in place past that point is now in the way.

Check yourself

Which is the best example of scaffolding?

No support to withdraw Giving the answer does the task for the learner. Nothing is built that can later come down.

Yes Progressive, differential and faded: all three properties of a scaffold.

That adds difficulty A harder task without support may land outside the zone.

No scaffold at all Struggle alone can push a learner toward rejection. The scaffold is the support.

Notice what this does to the algebra case. Leo could execute the procedure alone — that was inside his independent range. What he could not do alone was see what it was for.

That is a zone crossed by a peer, using a scaffold the teacher never designed.

Bronfenbrenner: the systems around the desk

The third disagreement is about scope (Bronfenbrenner, 1979). Development does not happen in a classroom; it happens in a set of nested systems, most of which the student never enters.

Trace it: the layoff (exo) → household income and stress (micro) → a rule about sketchbooks (micro) → a conversation about nursing as a stable career (macro — what counts as a real job) → a fourteen-year-old’s algebra grade.

None of the links in that chain is a choice Maya made.

True or false?

A parent’s workplace is part of a student’s microsystem.

Not quite It is the exosystem: a setting the student never enters that still reaches them, like Maya’s father’s layoff.

Right It is exosystem. The student never enters it, and it changes their day anyway.

That is not an argument that the grade is not her responsibility. It is an argument that a teacher who explains it entirely by her effort is working with a model missing four of its five levels.

They are not interchangeable

Three different answers to where does thinking come from — the individual acting on the world, the space between people, the systems nobody can see from inside the classroom.

You will need all three on Tuesday, and we will map the disagreements together then.

True or false?

Piaget, Vygotsky and Bronfenbrenner give three versions of the same explanation of development.

Not quite They disagree about where thinking comes from: the individual acting on the world, the space between people, or systems nobody sees from the classroom.

Right Three different answers. You need all three on Tuesday.

Check yourself

Check yourself

Leo could execute the quadratic formula for a month without knowing what it produced. After seeing Maya’s drawing, the formula “was about something.” The best description is:

The wrong direction Assimilation would mean the drawing was absorbed without changing anything. Something did change — the procedure acquired a referent it did not have before.

Half right, and worth thinking about He was arguably not in equilibrium — he had a procedure with no meaning attached, which is an unstable state students tolerate for a long time. But the more precise account is what resolved it, and that was social.

Yes He could do the steps alone. He could not, alone, see what they were for. A peer supplied a representation he could already read, and that put the meaning inside his reach — a ZPD crossed with a scaffold the teacher had not designed.

Nothing was rejected He kept the procedure — it just acquired meaning. Rejection means discarding information to protect an existing schema, which is not what happened here.

Check yourself

A teacher gives every student in the class the same set of sentence starters for a written task, all year, unchanged. The clearest problem is:

Not established Nothing here says the task is too hard. The problem is with the support, not the difficulty.

Yes Two failures at once. Not differential — identical support for students in different zones. Not faded — support that never withdraws stops being a scaffold and becomes a dependency. Fairness is the usual justification, and it is what makes this mistake so durable.

Plausible but not the clearest It might well happen. But it is a downstream consequence; the direct problem is the structure of the scaffold.

Wrong level This is a classroom decision — microsystem. The exosystem is the level the student never enters.

Bring to Tuesday Your answer to case question 4 — which theorist has most to say about Maya, and what they would say. Commit to one. You are not expected to be right.

One thing you can think now that you could not at fourteen — and a guess at what made the difference.
